sections_target.text: This method is used to determine the kinematic viscosity of petroleum oil products, whether transparent or opaque. The measurement method depends on estimating the time required for a given volume of liquid to flow at a given temperature in a tube of given dimensions under the effect of gravitational acceleration. The dynamic viscosity is calculated from the measured kinematic viscosity.

rows: This method is used to determine how far oils conform to the international viscosity classification. An increase in viscosity in used oils indicates: oil oxidation - increased impurities - mixing with a higher-viscosity oil. A decrease indicates: fuel contamination - mixing with a lower-viscosity oil.

It is the time required for a given volume of liquid to flow freely through a capillary tube under the effect of gravitational acceleration. Its unit of measurement is the stoke (cm²/s); note that measurement is in centistokes, 1 stoke = 100 centistokes.
Kinematic viscosity

(Sometimes called absolute viscosity): it equals the product of the kinematic viscosity × the density of the liquid, provided it is measured at the same temperature as the kinematic viscosity measurement. Its unit of measurement is the poise (g/cm·s).
Dynamic viscosity
The sample is taken in the correct manner mentioned above, in accordance with MPIS (Oil-013-r2).
Make sure the data on the sample are correct.
Make sure the sample is placed in its own box so that it is not exposed to sunlight and dust.
Make sure the sample bottle is dry (free of water and dust).
Make completely sure of the viscosity bath system and that the temperature at which measurement is required is set.
Wear a mask or protective face mask when using organic solvents (such as benzene) to clean the tools.
Do not leave any oil traces that fall on the floor; remove them.
Viscometer: the viscometer used is of calibrated glass, three-branch type BS/IP/SL(s)a, which measures the required viscosity with repeatability tolerance.
Size no.
Nominal constant, C
Capillary diameter, mm
Minimum flow times, sec
Minimum viscosity cst
Viscometer holder: usually made of stainless steel, used to hold the viscometer inside the water bath so that it is in a completely vertical position.

Temperature measuring device: thermometers are the most commonly used temperature measuring device, provided they are standard; modern thermometers must be calibrated before use to confirm that they are standard. Note that another device other than thermometers may be used to measure temperature, provided it is accurate.
Time measuring device: the stopwatch is the most common, provided it is divided into small subdivisions of not more than 0.2 s, with an accuracy of at least 0.5%.
Oil lifting device in the viscometer: a hand rubber pump fitted with a rubber hose.
Use viscometers that have been previously calibrated.
Viscometers

The thermometers used in the viscosity test must be calibrated by comparing them with standard thermometers to the nearest 0.01°C in the case of kinematic viscosity. Thermometers are tested by total immersion, i.e. the mercury bulb of the thermometer in the water bath, with the thermometer stem left at room temperature.
Thermometers
The stopwatch used must be calibrated and well adjusted.
Time gauges

Using a standard liquid: select from the previous table a viscometer with a flow time of at least 200 s at a suitable temperature, preferably 37.7°C (100°F), and a standard liquid of known, constant kinematic viscosity, and start determining the flow rate to the nearest 0.2 s, then calculate the viscometer constant C from the relation C = V/t, where: V is the viscosity of the standard liquid, cSt; t is the average flow time, sec.

Using a standard viscometer: select a petroleum oil with a flow time of at least 200 s in the standard viscometer and in the viscometer to be calibrated. Select a standard viscometer with a known constant C, or another viscometer calibrated by a standard viscometer. Place the standard viscometer together with the viscometer to be calibrated in the same water bath, measure the flow time of the oil used according to the steps mentioned above, then calculate the unknown constant from the relation: C1 = t2·C2/t1, where: C1 is the constant of the viscometer to be calibrated; t1 is the flow time to the nearest 0.2 s for the viscometer to be measured; C2 is the constant of the standard viscometer; t2 is the flow time to the nearest 0.2 s for the standard viscometer.

After the test is finished, clean the viscometer by emptying the oil into the designated container, then start cleaning by passing benzene through the three branches with gentle shaking, and so on until you are sure the viscometer is free of any traces of oil. Then dry the viscometer of any traces of benzene by passing a stream of dry air through the three branches of the viscometer for not less than 2 minutes.
Connect the viscosity apparatus to the electric power source and press the main power switch.
Using the selector switch, set it to the temperature required for measurement.
Leave the apparatus until the bath temperature reaches the required measurement temperature.
Meanwhile, select the suitable viscometer for measurement, record its constant, then place it in its holder.

Using a 50 ml beaker, fill the viscometer with the oil to be measured up to the mark, make sure it is free of any air bubbles and that there are no traces of oil on the outside of the viscometer, then place the viscometer in the viscosity bath so that the upper mark of the viscometer is 2 cm below the surface of the bath water, and wait 10-15 minutes until the oil takes the bath temperature (the required measurement temperature).
Place the hand pump hose in branch No. (1) of the viscometer, block branch No. (3) with your finger, then use the pump to raise the oil in branch No. (2) by 5 ml above the mark.
Let the oil flow in branch No. (2); when it reaches the upper measurement mark, press the stopwatch, and when the oil reaches the lower mark, press the stopwatch again, then calculate the time.
Repeat steps (7) and (8) to calculate the flow time a second time, provided the difference between the two times does not exceed 0.2 s, then calculate the average of the two times.
Calculate the viscosity using the equation cSt = C·T, where C is the viscometer constant and T is the average flow time.
The kinematic viscosity is calculated from the relation: Kinematic Viscosity, cSt = C·T, where: C is the viscometer factor or constant; T is the measured average flow time, sec.
The precision limits mentioned below apply only to pure transparent oils (free of impurities) tested at temperatures of 60 to 212°F (15 to 100°C).
Duplicate results obtained for the same oil using the same viscometer or another viscometer are considered valid unless the difference between their averages is greater than 0.35%.
Results obtained from two different laboratories (or even two different persons) are considered valid as long as the difference in the average of the results does not exceed 0.7%.

Introduction
This method is used to determine the kinematic viscosity of petroleum oil products, whether transparent or opaque. The measurement method depends on estimating the time required for a given volume of liquid to flow at a given temperature in a tube of given dimensions under the effect of gravitational acceleration. The dynamic viscosity is calculated from the measured kinematic viscosity.

Objective
This method is used to determine how far oils conform to the international viscosity classification. An increase in viscosity in used oils indicates: oil oxidation - increased impurities - mixing with a higher-viscosity oil. A decrease indicates: fuel contamination - mixing with a lower-viscosity oil.
